Portal hypertension: 4

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A patient with advanced portal hypertension has prominent radiating veins around the umbilicus. Which anatomical adaptation best explains this finding rather than interpreting it as a primary disease of the abdominal skin?

  1. Congestive splenomegaly and sequestration
  2. Portal-hypertensive ascites
  3. Portosystemic shunting contributing to encephalopathy
  4. Abdominal wall portosystemic collaterals
  5. Portosystemic gastroesophageal varices
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Abdominal wall portosystemic collaterals

Dilated periumbilical veins can reflect collateral flow in portal hypertension.

Understanding the options

Abdominal wall portosystemic collaterals
Dilated periumbilical veins can reflect collateral flow in portal hypertension.
Portosystemic gastroesophageal varices
Elevated portal pressure can dilate collateral veins and cause life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Congestive splenomegaly and sequestration
Portal hypertension can enlarge the spleen and contribute to thrombocytopenia. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Portal-hypertensive ascites
Portal pressure and sodium-retaining responses contribute to ascites. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Portosystemic shunting contributing to encephalopathy
Blood bypassing hepatic clearance can contribute to encephalopathy, including after TIPS. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
